facts.title: Hidden in zinc ore
facts.text: Cadmium was discovered in 1817 by the German chemist Friedrich Stromeyer, who noticed that some samples of zinc carbonate turned yellow when heated even though they contained no known impurity. Tracking the color down, he isolated a new metal hiding inside the zinc. To this day cadmium is produced almost entirely as a byproduct of refining zinc, since the two metals occur together in nature.

facts.title: Named after a Greek myth
facts.text: The name cadmium comes from 'cadmia', the ancient Latin and Greek word for zinc-bearing earths and calamine. That word in turn traces back to Cadmus, the legendary Phoenician prince of Greek mythology who founded the city of Thebes. So an element discovered in 1817 carries a name rooted in Bronze Age legend.

facts.title: A metal you can hear
facts.text: Cadmium is a soft, silvery-white metal so malleable it can be cut with a knife, much like its neighbor tin. Like tin, a bar of cadmium emits a faint crackling sound called the 'cadmium cry' when bent, caused by the rearrangement of its crystal structure. It melts at a relatively low 321 degrees Celsius and boils at 767 degrees Celsius.

facts.title: The color of great paintings
facts.text: Cadmium sulfide and cadmium selenide produce some of the most brilliant and durable yellow, orange, and red pigments ever made, known as the cadmium colors. Introduced commercially in the mid-1800s, they were prized by artists including Claude Monet, Vincent van Gogh, and Henri Matisse for their intense, fade-resistant hues. The exact shade depends on particle size and the ratio of sulfur to selenium.

facts.title: Powering rechargeable batteries
facts.text: For much of the 20th century, nickel-cadmium (NiCd) batteries were the dominant rechargeable cells, valued for delivering high current and surviving thousands of charge cycles. They powered early camcorders, power tools, and emergency lighting. Because of cadmium's toxicity, the European Union has largely banned NiCd batteries for consumer use since 2006, and they have been mostly replaced by nickel-metal-hydride and lithium-ion chemistries.

facts.title: A guardian inside reactors
facts.text: Cadmium is an excellent absorber of slow (thermal) neutrons, which makes it valuable for controlling nuclear chain reactions. Control rods containing cadmium, often alloyed with silver and indium, are inserted into reactor cores to soak up neutrons and slow or stop fission. A thin sheet of cadmium can block neutrons of a particular energy almost completely, a property physicists call the 'cadmium cutoff'.

facts.title: A surprisingly toxic twin of zinc
facts.text: Cadmium has no known biological function and is genuinely poisonous because it chemically mimics zinc and calcium, sneaking into enzymes and bones where those metals belong. Chronic exposure damages the kidneys and weakens bones, and it is classified as a human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. The body has no efficient way to excrete it, so it accumulates over a lifetime, with a biological half-life of decades.

facts.title: The itai-itai disaster
facts.text: In the early-to-mid 20th century, mining waste contaminated the Jinzu River basin in Toyama Prefecture, Japan, with cadmium that entered rice paddies and the food chain. Residents, especially older women who had borne children, developed an agonizing bone disease they named 'itai-itai' (Japanese for 'it hurts, it hurts'). It became one of the first documented cases of mass cadmium poisoning and a landmark in environmental health law.

facts.title: Forged in dying stars
facts.text: Cadmium's atoms are built in stars by the slow neutron-capture process, the s-process, which occurs in aging red giant stars as nuclei gradually absorb neutrons over thousands of years. The element has eight naturally occurring isotopes, an unusually high number. Two of them, cadmium-113 and cadmium-116, are technically radioactive but decay so slowly, with half-lives of trillions of years, that they are effectively stable.

facts.title: Glowing quantum dots
facts.text: Nanometer-sized crystals of cadmium selenide and cadmium telluride, called quantum dots, glow in precise colors that depend purely on their size, a vivid demonstration of quantum confinement. Larger dots emit red light and smaller ones emit blue, all from the same material. These cadmium-based dots powered the first generation of ultra-vivid QLED television displays and are used as fluorescent labels in biomedical imaging.
